transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I guess I came in because I feel like I’m worrying about practically everything lately, and it’s gotten to where I can tell it’s more than the situation really calls for. I worry about my clients, the market, whether a deal is going to fall through, whether I’ve missed something important. Then I go home and I’m worrying about my family, money, and even this move I made to the condo—whether that was the right decision or if I should’ve done something different.

It’s just… my mind keeps finding things to latch onto, even when nothing terrible is actually happening. I know some worry is normal, especially in real estate, but this feels out of proportion, like I can’t just take things as they come anymore.
Do these worries ever feel like unwanted thoughts that pop into your mind even when you don’t want them to?

Yes… I think that’s exactly what it feels like, though I don’t know if I’d call them “thoughts” so much as concerns that sort of barge in and then take over. Even when I tell myself, “Parin, this is not urgent, you don’t need to solve this right this second,” it doesn’t really stop there. One little thing will lead to another, and then another, and before I know it I’ve spent half an hour replaying some small detail I meant to let go.

Like I’ll think, did I phrase that email the wrong way, or should I have followed up differently, or what if that means something is going to fall apart later? And I know, rationally, it’s probably not worth all that time. But in the moment it feels hard to just… put it down. It’s unwanted in the sense that I’m tired of it and I don’t invite it, but it still keeps coming back.
When these worries show up, do you find yourself doing anything over and over—like checking, repeating, or mentally reviewing things—to try to feel less anxious?

I’m not sure I’d say I have a ritual exactly, like I don’t think I’m counting things or repeating a phrase or anything like that. But I do… sort of go back over things in my head, if that counts? Like I’ll replay a conversation or an email and think through what I said, what they might have thought, whether I should have handled it differently.

And sometimes I’ll look back at a message or a document again, but it doesn’t feel like a formal “I have to check this five times” kind of thing. It’s more that I’m trying to reassure myself, I guess, and then the reassurance doesn’t really last very long. I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean. It feels more like getting stuck than doing a specific repeated action.
Did this increase in worrying start after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

Yes… I think it did. It wasn’t like one dramatic day where everything changed all at once, but looking back, it really started after I sold my longtime house and moved into the condo. That was a big change for me, more emotional than I think I admitted at the time.

I’d lived in that house for so long, and the sale itself was a lot, then downsizing and trying to make the condo feel like home… after that, I started noticing the worrying was just more constant. So I’d say it’s been going on for about a year and two months now, roughly since that move.
When the worrying starts, is it hard for you to control or stop it?

Yes, it is. That’s actually the part that bothers me the most, I think. I can sometimes recognize that I’m doing it, and I’ll even say to myself, Parin, this is not urgent, you don’t need to figure this out right now. But it doesn’t really stop just because I’ve noticed it.

It’s like one concern hooks onto another one. I’ll start with one small thing, something I meant to just let go, and then my mind keeps building on it. Before I realize it, I’ve spent half an hour going over tiny details that probably don’t need that much attention. So yes, I can tell myself to stop, but actually stopping feels much harder than it should.
Aside from the move to the condo, are most of your worries mainly about that change in your life?

No, not only the condo. The move definitely seemed to set it off, or at least that’s when I noticed it getting worse, but now it feels like the worrying has spread into almost everything.

I’ll worry about clients and whether I handled something correctly, or the market and whether things are going to shift in a way I should have anticipated. Then it’ll be my family, or money, or some decision I made earlier in the day. And yes, I still circle back to the condo—whether selling the house was the right choice, whether I rushed it, whether I should have done something differently—but it’s not contained to that.

That’s part of why I came in, really. It feels out of proportion to what’s actually happening. Nothing has to be actively going wrong for my mind to start searching for something to worry about.
Have you been feeling restless or on edge a lot of the time?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I wouldn’t say I’m pacing around or unable to sit still all the time, if that’s what you mean by restless. But “on edge”… maybe sometimes, yes. It’s more like I have this sense that I should be doing something or checking something, even when there isn’t anything specific happening.

It’s not constant every minute, and I don’t know if I’d call it severe. I can still sit with clients or get through my day. But there are times when I feel a little keyed up inside, like I’m waiting for something to need my attention. I’ve sort of thought of it as just being responsible or alert, so I haven’t really tracked it as a symptom.
Do you often notice your muscles feeling tense?

Yes, I do, actually. I notice it most at the end of the day. My neck and shoulders will feel really tight, almost like I’ve been holding myself in a braced position without realizing it. It’s not like I’m lifting heavy things all day, so sometimes I’ll think, why do I feel so stiff?

And I’ve started catching myself clenching my jaw, especially when I’m driving between listings or sitting at my desk going through paperwork. I’ll suddenly realize my teeth are pressed together, and then I have to consciously relax my face. I don’t always notice it while it’s happening, but by later in the day it’s pretty obvious in my shoulders and neck.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes, I have. Not every night in exactly the same way, but most nights I do get into bed at a reasonable hour—I’m not staying up watching television or anything like that—and then once I’m lying there, my mind just starts going.

It’s like I’ll think, okay, I need to sleep, and then suddenly I’m running through the condo fees, or whether I have everything lined up for tomorrow’s showings, or I’ll remember some contract detail and start wondering if I missed something or should have worded something differently. One thought leads to another, and before I know it I’ve been lying there much longer than I meant to.

I do eventually sleep, but it doesn’t feel very restful. I wake up feeling like I never quite fully settled down, if that makes sense—like my body was in bed, but my mind didn’t really shut off.
Do you often feel easily tired?

I’m not sure I’d say “easily tired,” exactly. I mean, I do get tired, but I’ve also always had fairly full days, so sometimes it’s hard for me to know what’s normal tired and what’s more than that.

There are days where by late afternoon I feel a little worn down, like I don’t have quite as much energy left for the next phone call or errand, but I can usually keep going. I’m not falling asleep at my desk or needing naps every day or anything like that. It’s more that I feel kind of drained sometimes, but I haven’t really separated that out as its own thing. I guess I’ve mostly chalked it up to work and age and just being busy.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yes, I have noticed that, especially with paperwork. It’s not constant, but when I’m reviewing purchase agreements or inspection addendums, I’ll be reading a paragraph that I really do need to pay attention to, and then some worry will pop into my head—like whether I missed a detail somewhere else or what needs to happen next—and suddenly I realize I have no idea what I just read.

So I’ll go back and read the same paragraph again, and sometimes even three or four times, because I keep losing the thread of what I was checking. It’s frustrating, because these are documents I’m used to reading. It’s not that I don’t understand them. It’s more like my attention gets pulled off track by whatever I’m worrying about, and then I have to keep starting over.
Do you ever feel driven to check something repeatedly to relieve the anxiety?

I don’t think so, not in that sense. I mean, I do check things because my work kind of requires it—contracts, dates, lockbox codes, appointment times, that sort of thing—but I wouldn’t say I’m driven to do it over and over until the anxiety goes away.

Sometimes I’ll look back at an email or a document again if I’m uneasy about it, just to make sure I didn’t miss something, but it’s not like I have a ritual or a number of times I need to check. And I don’t think checking gives me some big relief so much as it’s just me trying to be careful. I may second-guess myself more than I used to, but repeated checking… no, I don’t think that’s really a major thing for me.
